title: Skin and pressure care with arthritis and frailty (UK)
meta_title: Skin and pressure care with arthritis and frailty (UK)
meta_description: Pressure care with arthritis and frailty: daily skin checks, changes on darker skin, movement and equipment plans, and when to get urgent help.
excerpt: A practical guide to pressure care when arthritis and frailty make moving difficult, with skin changes to report, equipment questions and urgent-help routes.
direct_answer: If arthritis or frailty makes changing position difficult, ask your GP for a pressure-ulcer risk assessment. Move as your individual plan advises and check skin daily. A persistent red, purple or blue patch needs attention. Hot or swollen skin, pus, fever or severe or worsening pain needs urgent advice.
author: Louis Maxwell
keywords: pressure ulcers, skin care, pressure sores, arthritis, frailty, UK
content:
If arthritis makes it difficult to shift your weight, get out of a chair or turn in bed, the same patches of skin may stay under pressure. Frailty can make those movements harder still. Pressure ulcers are damage to the skin and tissue underneath, not an inevitable part of getting older.

This Living With Arthritis guide explains what to look for, when to ask for an assessment and how to make a practical prevention plan. It does not replace a nurse's assessment, wound treatment or an individual moving-and-handling plan.

Quick answer: how can you protect your skin?

Change position regularly, check your skin every day and ask for a risk assessment if moving is difficult. A care team can advise about suitable cushions, mattresses and help with movement. Contact your GP if you think a pressure ulcer is developing. Hot or swollen skin, pus, fever, or severe or worsening pain needs urgent advice, not just a different cushion.

What does a pressure ulcer look or feel like?

The NHS pressure ulcer guide describes persistent discoloured patches, changes in skin texture and pain or itching. Common sites include the heels, elbows, hips and tailbone, where bone is close to the skin.

  • On white skin, a patch may look red and not change colour when pressed.
  • On brown or black skin, a change may look purple or blue rather than red.
  • The area may feel unusually warm, hard or spongy.
  • There may be pain or itching, a blister or an open wound.

Colour alone is not enough to judge every skin problem. Look for a change from the person's usual skin and notice how it feels. Reduced feeling can also make pain an unreliable warning. The NHS lists problems with sensation, poor circulation and fragile skin among the factors that increase risk.

Pressure damage can sometimes develop within hours. If you are unsure what a patch means, ask a healthcare professional rather than waiting for it to become an open wound.

When should you ask for help?

Contact your GP if you think you or someone you care for has a pressure ulcer. Do not try to diagnose its depth or choose wound treatment from a photograph. Tell the practice when the change started, where it is and whether the person can move away from pressure.

Ask for an urgent GP appointment or get help from NHS 111 if there are pressure-ulcer symptoms with hot, swollen or red skin, pus, a high temperature, severe pain or pain that is worsening. Inflamed skin can look blue or purple on brown or black skin. These are the NHS urgent-care signs.

In England, Scotland and Wales, use 111 where appropriate if you cannot get urgent advice from the practice. In Northern Ireland, contact your GP or GP out-of-hours service. Do not wait for a routine equipment review when the concern is a possible infection.

Call 999 or go to A&E if you think the person may have sepsis. The NHS sepsis guide includes new confusion or speech that does not make sense, very fast breathing, and blue, pale or blotchy skin among emergency signs in adults. Not everyone has every symptom. Do not drive yourself to A&E.

Why do arthritis and frailty make prevention harder?

Pressure comes from staying on the same area of skin or from something rubbing it. Arthritis may make a position comfortable for a joint but difficult to change. A person may be able to stand sometimes but not reliably turn in bed or reposition when tired. A chair that feels supportive does not remove the need to consider pressure.

The useful question is not only “Can you walk?” It is “Can you change position when you need to, including at night or on a difficult day?” Tell the assessor about those differences. Explain if hand or shoulder pain makes it hard to push up from a chair, or if a sore hip stops you turning onto one side.

Practical tip: Describe your most difficult part of the day, not only what you can do during an appointment. A plan needs to work when pain, fatigue or available help changes.

What belongs in a pressure-care plan?

If you are being cared for at home and think you are at risk, the NHS advises asking a GP for a risk assessment. A care team can then make a prevention plan. NICE patient guidance explains repositioning and pressure-redistributing equipment. Do not assume that a general turning timetable online is the right one for your skin, mobility and equipment.

  • Movement: which position changes you can do, which need help and how often they are needed.
  • Skin checks: which areas to check and who will help with areas you cannot see.
  • Equipment: whether a particular cushion or mattress is needed and how to use it.
  • Daily care: how to manage wet clothing, bedding or dressings and when to report a concern.
  • Contact arrangements: who to call for new damage, worsening symptoms or equipment problems.

If moving someone has become unsafe, do not improvise a lift or drag them across a surface. Ask the care team to review the method and support needed. A carer should not be expected to carry out a move they have not been shown how to do safely. The NHS moving and handling guide explains why training and professional advice matter.

How can you make daily skin checks manageable?

Choose a regular opportunity, such as getting dressed, when the skin can be seen without rushing. Ask permission before helping another person and protect their privacy. Explain any change calmly rather than suggesting that they have done something wrong.

A mirror may help you look at a heel, but it is not useful if holding it makes you unsteady. Ask for help with an area you cannot check. Do not rub or massage a discoloured area to try to prevent a pressure ulcer. NICE warns that this can damage fragile skin. If someone already has reduced feeling or cannot describe discomfort, tell the clinician how checks are being done.

Record a new change in ordinary words: its location, when you noticed it, whether the skin is broken, and whether there is warmth, swelling, pain or discharge. Recording is useful for a discussion, but it must not delay urgent help.

Will a pressure cushion or mattress solve the problem?

Specially designed cushions and mattresses are among the treatments and prevention measures described by the NHS. They need to be part of the plan, not a reason to stop checking skin or changing position.

Ask which equipment is suitable, how to position it and whom to contact if it is uncomfortable or stops working. Explain any difficulty standing from the chair or getting into bed. Equipment needs to work with those tasks as well as pressure care. Do not assume that any product labelled “orthopaedic” or “memory foam” is the equipment your assessor means.

Funding and provision depend on the assessment and local arrangements. Ask the service what it will supply and what you would need to arrange yourself before buying something on the assumption that it will be reimbursed.

What else supports prevention?

The NHS recommends staying active where possible and eating a healthy, balanced diet alongside regular position changes and daily skin checks. This is not a demand to exercise through severe pain or to follow a special “healing diet”. Ask your healthcare team for individual help if appetite, swallowing, weight loss or difficulty preparing food is affecting what you can eat.

Tell the team if wet skin, continence problems or fragile skin make care difficult. The assessment can consider the whole situation. If a pressure ulcer has already developed, a clinician may recommend dressings, creams, antibiotics or other treatment depending on its severity. Do not select those treatments from this prevention guide.

Remember: Pressure damage is not a failure by the person or their carer. Ask for a plan that is realistic about pain, movement and available help.

Key takeaways

  • Daily skin checks need to consider colour, warmth, texture and symptoms, not redness alone.
  • A suitable cushion or mattress supports, rather than replaces, position changes and assessment.
  • New skin damage needs attention. Infection signs need urgent advice and possible sepsis needs emergency help.

Frequently asked questions

Can a pressure ulcer happen even if I can walk?

Yes. Being able to walk at some times does not mean you can change position often enough at other times. Describe time spent sitting or lying and any difficulty moving.

Does it always look red?

No. Purple or blue changes can be more relevant on brown or black skin. Also notice warmth, texture, pain and changes from the person's usual skin.

Should I wait for broken skin before asking for help?

No. A persistent discoloured area or other concerning change can need assessment before there is an open wound.

How often should I turn?

Ask for an individual plan. The right support and timing depend on the assessment, skin condition, mobility and equipment, not a single schedule for everyone.

Can I just buy a cushion?

A cushion may be useful, but choosing one is not a substitute for assessment when there is skin damage or difficulty changing position. Ask about suitable equipment.

Who should I call if pain or discharge gets worse?

Seek an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 advice for severe or worsening pain, pus, hot or swollen skin or fever with pressure-ulcer symptoms. Possible sepsis needs emergency help.

Make the next step specific

If you have no skin damage but struggle to move, ask about a risk assessment. If you have noticed a possible pressure ulcer, contact your GP. If infection or emergency signs are present, use the urgent routes above. A useful plan makes clear who will help, what they will do and whom to call when something changes.

Sources and related guides

NHS pressure ulcers, NHS sepsis, NICE prevention guidance and NHS moving and handling.

Read wound care when reaching is difficult for minor-cut guidance. Pressure ulcers need their own assessment, not simply the same treatment as a cut.
